newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shekel down but not out, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shekel down but not out, analysts say.

text.p: The Israeli shekel has taken a strong beating in three days of trading, but most economists on Tuesday said the currency's downside potential appeared limited.

At its nadir on Tuesday, the shekel was trading at 3.55 shekels to the dollar, against 3.484 on Monday and 3.419 last Thursday. The shekel's representative rate against a basket of currencies was set at 3.5060.
"It's really hard when the pack is moving to say when it will stop," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets.

"The market will be very erratic in the next few days or week, but the fundamentals are still for a strong shekel," said Katz, who predicted the exchange rate would be at 3.50-3.55 shekels per dollar in a month's time.
The nervousness and uncertainty in the market follows last week's monetary measures.

The Israeli cabinet approved a foreign exchange reform that widened the upper limit of the shekel's trading band but not the lower limit. It also decreased the rate at which the lower diagonal limit will rise over a year.
The shekel depreciates as it moves towards the band's upper limit and appreciates as it approaches the lower limit.

Reducing the diagonal rate lowers the minimum shekel depreciation guaranteed by the Bank of Israel. But the widening of the top end of the band increases the risk of a substantial shekel depreciation.
Right after the measures were announced, the Bank of Israel lowered its key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points to an annual 12.7 percent.

The cut was widely seen as easing pressure on the shekel to appreciate. High interest rates had buoyed the currency, which for most of the year had traded at the lower limit of its band as the private sector converted foreign currency-linked loans into shekels to take advantage of the interest rate gap.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Tuesday such loans were less appealing under the current currency regime combined with lower rates.

"It could very well be that some of the people who thought it worthwhile to take loans in foreign currency, invest in shekel (deposits) and receive the high interest rate could now be taking into account that perhaps the interest rate on shekels is a little less high than what it was in the past and perhaps not worthwhile to them," Frenkel told Israel's army radio.
Much of the shekel's recent rapid decline has been the result of speculators, including foreigners, rushing to cover their positions, dealers said.
Speculation before the cabinet's decision had focused on expectations that any reform would expand both limits, which would have allowed the shekel to appreciate further.

"Speculators smelled an opportunity to make a big killing. They sold dollars in the hope that as a result of the government's decision they could buy dollars back at a cheaper level. They got burned and had to close their positions as quickly as possible," said Ilan Doron, also of Solid.
Katz predicted that if the shekel weakened further, nearing the middle of its band, it would again become advantageous to take out foreign currency-linked loans.
Israel Discount Bank chief economist Shauli Katznelson said the foreign currency reform had increased the likelihood of market volatility, raising the level of risk involved.
"Will people be more careful in taking short positions? If so, we will see a decline in the flow of foreign currency into Israel and the shekel will depreciate," Katznelson said.
But he did not foresee any major devaluation.
"Otherwise, the Bank of Israel will raise interest rates to contain inflation," said Katznelson, who predicted such a move would take place long before the shekel reached the upper limit of the band.
